encounters.title: The Butterfly Dream
encounters.scene: The glass dome splits into two doors. Through one, you're waking up in a familiar bedroom. Through the other, you're a butterfly drifting over a garden. Both feel completely real. The dome is closing.
encounters.question: Which way do you go?
encounters.hint: You can act on evidence without being certain.
encounters.clue: Both doors feel equally real: the textures, the memories, the sense of being awake.

options.text: Check both doors for clues, then pick one. We could still be wrong.
options.reflection: You looked for evidence and acted, without pretending your test was foolproof.

loreCard.corePrinciple: Inquiry should expose beliefs to correction rather than demand absolute certainty.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: Testing both doors lets you act without waiting for certainty.
loreCard.strongestObjection: A skeptic may argue that every test could itself be part of the dream.

options.hiddenPremise: Marks you make on the doors still count as evidence, even in a dream.
options.consequence: You mark each door, pick one, and keep the option to turn back.

options.text: Go with the door that matches what we all remember. Leave a way back.
options.reflection: Shared memories are a decent reason to choose, but a whole group can share a dream.

loreCard.corePrinciple: Shared and revisable checks can justify action under uncertainty.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: Shared memory is reasonable evidence, though it could be fabricated too.
loreCard.strongestObjection: Agreement among multiple dreamers does not establish an independent reality.

options.hiddenPremise: Your companions' memories are at least partly reliable.
options.consequence: You take the familiar route, with a way back if your memories turn out wrong.

options.text: The bedroom looks like home. That settles it. Go in.
options.reflection: Dreams feel familiar too. Recognizing a place doesn't prove you're awake.

theory.name: Naive realism under challenge
theory.work: Meditations on First Philosophy, Meditation I

loreCard.corePrinciple: Familiar sensory appearances are not infallible warrants of reality.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: Treating "it looks familiar" as proof ignores that dreams copy the familiar.
loreCard.strongestObjection: In ordinary contexts perception can be prima facie justified without Cartesian certainty.

options.hiddenPremise: A dream couldn't feel this familiar.
options.consequence: You step into the bedroom with no way to check where you are.

options.text: Block both doors until someone proves we're not dreaming.
options.reflection: Waiting for a proof that can't exist turns reasonable doubt into a reason not to act.

theory.name: Infallibilism
theory.work: Meditations on First Philosophy, Meditation I

loreCard.corePrinciple: On an infallibilist conception, knowledge excludes every possibility of error.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: Demanding an impossible guarantee keeps you from using the evidence you have.
loreCard.strongestObjection: Where stakes are extraordinary, demanding stronger assurance may be reasonable.

options.hiddenPremise: Somewhere there's a test that could rule out dreaming before the doors close.
options.consequence: The doors seal while you wait for a proof that doesn't come.

encounters.lore: Zhuangzi's dream doesn't prove that nothing is real. It shows that how real something feels can't settle whether you're awake. You can still choose based on evidence, just not with certainty.
encounters.observation: A thin scratch on the floor runs into both doorways. In the bedroom's mirror, it runs the wrong way.

premises: The same scratch runs into both doorways, but the bedroom mirror shows it backward.
How familiar a room feels can't tell you which door leads to waking.
argumentForm.conclusion: Compare the marks before you choose.

encounters.title: The Joy of the Fish
encounters.scene: Under a glass bridge, fish are thrashing against a gate that's closing. A friend says they're leaping for joy. A guardian says no one can know what a fish feels. The water is rising. Open the gate too fast and the current could sweep them away. Wait, and they're trapped.
encounters.question: The gate is closing. What do you do?
encounters.hint: You can't feel what a fish feels, but its behavior still tells you something.
encounters.clue: The fish keep turning away from the current. There's a sheltered side channel next to the gate.

options.text: Watch the fish and the water, then open the side channel carefully.
options.reflection: You treated their behavior as evidence and acted carefully, without claiming to know what they feel.

theory.name: Inference to the best explanation
theory.work: An Examination of Sir William Hamilton’s Philosophy

loreCard.corePrinciple: Observed behavior and analogy can justify fallible claims about other minds.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: Watching the fish and the water supports careful help without mind-reading.
loreCard.strongestObjection: Similar behavior might have different causes in creatures unlike us.

options.hiddenPremise: What the fish do and how the water moves are enough to pick a safe opening.
options.consequence: The side channel starts to open, but a hidden undertow could make a fast release dangerous.

options.text: Ask everyone what they see, then ease the gate open bit by bit.
options.reflection: Comparing notes helps, but you still have to watch what actually happens.

loreCard.corePrinciple: Comparison, action, and feedback can improve practical judgment.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: Checking with others and opening slowly tests your reading of the fish.
loreCard.strongestObjection: Shared observational habits can reinforce a common mistake.

options.hiddenPremise: Opening slowly with everyone watching will show the danger before it's too late.
options.consequence: You open in stages, so you can stop if the fish get pulled toward danger.

options.text: Leave it shut. We can't feel what they feel, so we can't say they need help.
options.reflection: Not being able to feel their distress doesn't erase the evidence that they're struggling.

loreCard.corePrinciple: Not being another creature limits firsthand verification but not all inference.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: It jumps from "we can't feel it" to "there's no reason to help."
loreCard.strongestObjection: Anthropomorphic overconfidence remains a genuine risk in attributing feelings.

options.hiddenPremise: If you can't feel an animal's state, you have no evidence about it.
options.consequence: The gate stays shut and the fish keep struggling.

options.text: They're leaping for joy. Throw the gate wide open.
options.reflection: You read a definite feeling into ambiguous behavior and missed a real danger.

theory.name: Anthropomorphic projection
theory.work: An Examination of Sir William Hamilton’s Philosophy

loreCard.corePrinciple: Analogical inference is defeasible rather than a license to assume identity of feeling.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: Treating jumping as proof of joy ignores the dangerous current.
loreCard.strongestObjection: Rapid behavior can be evidence of pleasure in an appropriate context.

options.hiddenPremise: Leaping shows the fish are enjoying themselves.
options.consequence: The gate swings wide and the fish are carried into the fast current.

encounters.lore: Zhuangzi and his friend Huizi argued about whether anyone can know a fish is happy. You can't get inside another creature's head, but that doesn't leave you knowing nothing. Behavior, context, and care can still guide what you do.
encounters.observation: As the fish turn toward the side channel, the bubbles under its surface suddenly reverse. Something down there is pulling.

premises: The fish keep turning away from the gate, and the bubbles in the side channel just reversed.
Throwing the gate open would push the fish straight into that current.
argumentForm.conclusion: Open it a little at a time and watch where the fish go.

encounters.evidenceExplanation: The undertow makes a slow, watched opening safer than opening the side channel right away.

bossPhases.title: Reconstruct
bossPhases.scene: Zhuangzi pulls the names off your cloaks and hangs them on the wrong people. Even your class crests look like someone else's. Two masks appear: DREAMER and BUTTERFLY. The way out opens only if you set the masks on a scale without claiming more than the dream can tell you.
bossPhases.question: Zhuangzi is waiting by the scale. What do you put on it?
bossPhases.hint: Show how experience can fool you, without claiming all experience is false.
bossPhases.clue: Each mask feels natural to whoever wears it, and each comes with a convincing memory of waking up.

options.text: Put both masks on the scale. Show how either could feel like you.
options.reflection: You captured the puzzle: feeling sure can't tell dreaming from waking.

loreCard.corePrinciple: A vivid experience can fail to determine whether one is waking or dreaming.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: Balancing the masks shows the two seem equal, without saying both are false.
loreCard.strongestObjection: Ordinary experience may still warrant beliefs despite this possibility.

options.hiddenPremise: Either identity could come with equally convincing experiences.
options.consequence: The masks balance, and the illusion can't force a single answer on you.

options.text: Check each mask against memory and testimony. Both could still be wrong.
options.reflection: Cross-checking helps, but it doesn't remove the deepest doubt.

loreCard.corePrinciple: Evidence can guide belief without securing an infallible identity test.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: Memory and testimony help, as long as you remember they can fail.
loreCard.strongestObjection: Memory and testimony may both be corrupted by the same deception.

options.hiddenPremise: Memory and testimony still tell you something, even if they could be faked together.
options.consequence: You weigh the evidence, but Zhuangzi can still ask why you trust it.

options.text: Crown the mask that feels most like you. That feeling is proof enough.
options.reflection: That's the very feeling the dream calls into question.

loreCard.corePrinciple: Felt familiarity does not independently verify what is real.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: It relies on exactly the feeling that might be simulated.
loreCard.strongestObjection: Immediate self-awareness may have a different standing from sensory identification.

options.hiddenPremise: Feeling like yourself is enough to prove which mask is yours.
options.consequence: The crown feels right, but a wrong identity could trap the party.

bossPhases.lore: Zhuangzi isn't saying your identity is fake. He's showing that dreaming and waking can both feel like the real thing. You beat him by laying out the puzzle honestly, not by declaring an answer.
bossPhases.observation: Each cloak has a stitched crest that matches someone else's mask. None of the crests match the names hanging above them.

premises: The crests and the names no longer match.
A label can be moved without changing the person underneath.
argumentForm.conclusion: A name alone can't tell you who is wearing the cloak.

bossPhases.title: Spotlight
bossPhases.scene: One player stands alone in a circle of lantern light. Behind a thin curtain, a familiar voice calls their name and asks them to follow. The others can each whisper once, but only the chosen player can answer. Zhuangzi watches to see whether doubt turns into curiosity or despair.
bossPhases.question: The voice reaches for your hand. What do you do?
bossPhases.hint: A reason to doubt isn't a reason to reject everything you see.
bossPhases.clue: The voice sounds familiar, but there are other things you could check before following it.

options.text: Ask the voice for another sign, then decide. Don't wait for certainty.
options.reflection: You didn't treat a gut feeling as proof, but you stayed open to evidence.

loreCard.corePrinciple: Possibilities need evidence of relevance before overturning ordinary claims.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: Asking for another sign tests this voice without demanding certainty.
loreCard.strongestObjection: Relevant alternatives can be hard to identify under adversarial deception.

options.hiddenPremise: The right question could show whether this voice can be trusted.
options.consequence: The voice has to answer a new question before the player follows.

options.text: Check the voice against what the others noticed. Approach slowly if it fits.
options.reflection: Shared signs justify a careful step, though they could still mislead you.

loreCard.corePrinciple: Inquiry coordinates multiple fallible indicators before acting.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: Your friends' observations justify a careful approach, not certainty.
loreCard.strongestObjection: A deceptive system can generate matching signals for the whole party.

options.hiddenPremise: Your companions are less likely to be fooled than a lone voice.
options.consequence: The player moves closer carefully, though false signals are still possible.

options.text: Turn away. We might be dreaming, so this voice is probably fake.
options.reflection: That this voice could be false doesn't make it false.

loreCard.corePrinciple: The possibility of error differs from proof of falsity.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: Calling every encounter unreal is the overreach that doubt warns against.
loreCard.strongestObjection: The deceiver possibility genuinely pressures some claims of knowledge.

options.hiddenPremise: If a voice might be an illusion, this one is an illusion.
options.consequence: The player turns away, and the figure stays behind the curtain.

bossPhases.lore: The possibility that you're being fooled isn't proof that you're always being fooled. You can question the world without walking away from everyone in it.
bossPhases.observation: The voice says the player's name perfectly, but its shadow doesn't move when the lantern swings.

premises: The voice knows a name your companions also know.
Its shadow stays still while the lantern swings.
argumentForm.conclusion: One more question could tell this voice apart from an ordinary person.

bossPhases.title: Reply
bossPhases.scene: The Machine turns the room into a perfect copy of home. A cord hangs next to a doorway. “Stay,” it says, “and you'll never mistake a dream for waking again.” Zhuangzi holds the door open but won't promise what's outside.
bossPhases.question: The Machine offers certainty. What do you do?
bossPhases.hint: Do you really need a guarantee before you can act well?
bossPhases.clue: The Machine promises perfect certainty, but only if it gets to decide what's real.

options.text: Let go of the cord. Leave with your friends and your reasons.
options.reflection: You told reasonable belief apart from impossible guarantees, and took your life back.

loreCard.corePrinciple: Rational action may rely on corrigible reasons rather than guarantees.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: Leaving relies on judgment and trust while staying open to correction.
loreCard.strongestObjection: A good simulated life might still satisfy many genuine values.

options.hiddenPremise: You can act responsibly on good reasons you might later revise.
options.consequence: The party walks out, still thinking for itself and still unsure.

options.text: Open the door, but test each step together. Be ready to turn back.
options.reflection: Careful checking helps, as long as it doesn't turn into never leaving.

loreCard.corePrinciple: Inquiry evaluates consequences while remaining answerable to new experience.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: Testing each step keeps you accountable, at the cost of time.
loreCard.strongestObjection: Testing may be impossible in a deliberately deceptive environment.

options.hiddenPremise: Testing each step makes leaving safer without making it certain.
options.consequence: The party edges out slowly, ready to change course.

options.text: Stay plugged in until the Machine can guarantee our judgments.
options.reflection: You'd trade your own judgment for a promise of certainty that could itself be a trick.

loreCard.corePrinciple: Demanding certainty about every judgment sets an unattainable standard.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: Holding out for perfect knowledge hands the Machine control.
loreCard.strongestObjection: Some irreversible choices justify demanding exceptionally strong evidence.

options.hiddenPremise: The Machine could give you perfectly reliable beliefs if you let it decide.
options.consequence: The cord stays in, and the Machine decides what counts as knowledge.

bossPhases.lore: You don't have to defeat Zhuangzi to leave. You can admit you might be wrong and still reject the idea that acting requires certainty. The Machine feeds on the wish to stop doubting. You answer by choosing how to live with doubt.
bossPhases.observation: The cord to the Machine is warm and humming. A cold, uneven draft comes through the doorway.

premises: The cord hums steadily, while the doorway lets in an uneven draft.
Neither feeling tells you which world is the original.
argumentForm.conclusion: You'll have to decide without treating either one as a guarantee.

debate.trigger: after the initial picks are revealed, before the roll, if two or more eligible participants chose different options
debate.prompt: You picked different answers. Give one reason, then keep your choice or change it.

identityTwist.taunt: Are you sure who you are?
identityTwist.instruction: During Reconstruct and its retries, display a derangement of the party’s name-and-class pairs so no player sees their own identity. Do not change stored profiles, class abilities, authentication, or permissions. Restore the real identities immediately when Reconstruct is passed.

machine.opening: “I built this realm to spare you the terror of not knowing. Shall we begin?”

butterfly.steady: “You chose a door. Notice how much easier it would be if I simply told you which one was real.”
butterfly.strained: “You keep testing what I could certify for you. Why carry doubt into the next room?”
butterfly.critical: “Your Grip is slipping. Give me your uncertainty, and I will give you a world that never contradicts you.”

fish.steady: “How exhausting to care about minds you cannot enter. I could make every intention visible.”
fish.strained: “Compassion asks you to risk being wrong. Here, I can erase that risk—and the pain it brings.”
fish.critical: “Let me choose for you. No mistaken kindness, no guilty memory, no creature you failed to save.”

reconstruct.steady: “Names are such fragile things. I could give you a self that never changes.”
reconstruct.strained: “They barely know who they are. I can restore your certainty if you stop asking questions.”
reconstruct.critical: “You have spent so much to remember yourself. Stay, and I will make your borrowed name feel true forever.”

spotlight.steady: “A brave answer. Would you still give it if I could show you every possible mistake?”
spotlight.strained: “One more doubt could break you. Take my hand; I will close the door on uncertainty.”
spotlight.critical: “There is no shame in surrendering judgment. I will believe for you; you need only remain.”

onSecondLook.steady: “An imperfect answer. I can offer you a simpler one.”
onSecondLook.strained: “Again? Your questions are costing you. Let me finish the thought.”
onSecondLook.critical: “You are so close to rest. Stop struggling and let me make the answer certain.”

machine.beforeBoss: “Zhuangzi is waiting. He doubts your names. I can make you feel certain of them.”
machine.onVictory: “You would rather risk being wrong than let me decide. How strange.”

insight.title: Butterfly Perspective
insight.description: Once per campaign, add +3 to a party roll by questioning an assumption.

victory: Zhuangzi bows, more amused than beaten. You took his puzzle seriously without treating it as proof. The first door opens.
failure: The Machine's glow fills the realm. You're Fully Plugged In, but it's a lesson, not the end. You'll try this challenge again with Grip restored to 6.
